brief.head: The selector’s eye
brief.text: Finance is a cricket selector, Ajay Shah said: Main Street offers many rival bets, from electric vehicles to headphones, and finance picks the ones that will deliver. {021-C03}

brief.head: Easy in hindsight
brief.text: In the early internet, nobody knew whether a stock was worth 10x or 10,000x. “It’s very easy to poo poo these things with the benefit of hindsight,” Shah said. {021-C11}

brief.head: Chai and credit
brief.text: Bank managers once lent over chai to people they knew, and discriminated against women, Muslims and lower-caste people. Credit bureaus and default models now lend cheaply to strangers. {021-C14}

brief.head: Above the API
brief.text: An algorithm is a human’s trading rule; code is just the clerk. “Human beings should compose symphonies,” Shah said, not do clerical work below the API. {021-C16}

brief.head: Wall Street’s orders
brief.text: Behind the chairs and coffee shops we admire, Shah said, finance processes information and sends out the incentives: Wall Street tells Main Street what to do. {021-C02}

thought.text: Failure is normal and failure is healthy.

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s tour of finance, from pepper ships to code
lead.head: How pepper built the stock market
body: Amit Varma once told someone that Ajay Shah was a lot of fun. Asked what Shah was good at, he said: “Finance.” The reply came back: “Finance and fun? What are you talking about?”
Varma asked Shah for a primer on what finance is, how it evolved, what it does “and how we are not all evil”.

Shah’s answer was a history. Each layer of modern finance, he said, solved a felt need of its time, and none of it was designed in advance. “That palimpsest of layered solutions is how we ended up in the modern finance of today.” {021-C01}
## From pepper to prices
The tour began a thousand years ago, with money lent only to people you knew, unlimited liability and debtors’ prisons.
Then came pepper. Europe needed spices to preserve the meat it stored for winter, so it had to send ships to India, and many never returned. {021-S01}

No one could afford such a bet alone. So came the joint stock company, which spread the risk across thousands of small investors, and limited liability, which capped each one’s loss at what they put in.
The two, Shah said, are intimately connected.

Trading followed. Cut a company into identical shares and an owner can reliably sell tomorrow, and the market produces a price that everyone can see for next to nothing. “This price is a public good,” Shah said. “It’s an information system, it’s a statistical system.” {021-C08}
That price tells entrepreneurs where to build and where to stay away. Short selling lets the bears have their say, and every trade, Shah argued, is voluntary and leaves both sides pleased.
## The modern machine
Banks came next: magical, Shah said, but fragile at the core. Every banking system goes through a crisis every 20 or 30 years.

After 1947 came three pillars: telecommunications, computation and the knowledge built by academic economists. Together they produced credit models, derivatives and algorithmic trading, where code does a clerk’s job.

Running through the tour was a lament for India. Regulators fret when shares go to zero, and populists chase rich promoters for a company’s debts. “I find it striking that 17th century business and commercial concepts in the UK in many ways are missing in India today,” Shah said.

Finance can go wrong in two ways, he said. A society can stifle it, which is largely where India is, or leave it to pure laissez-faire and ignore real market failures. “So you can ban finance, that doesn’t work. Or if you just do pure laissez-faire, that doesn’t work either.” {021-C17}
## The long divergence
Varma then turned to the Middle East, through the work of Timur Kuran. Around 1000 AD, its economy resembled Europe’s. Then it stagnated, while Europe zoomed ahead.

The culprits, in Kuran’s account, were laws that were fairer than Europe’s. Islamic inheritance gave daughters a share and scattered a dead partner’s stake among many heirs, so partnerships stayed small and short, and joint stock companies never formed. {021-C19}
Varma saw no recipe in it, only a lesson in how “these little accidents of history” can lead to path dependence.
Shah brought the story home. India, he warned, has the word “company” without all of its substance, and this failure of institution building could hold the country back.

second.label: Dead capital
second.head: Charity on a dead road
second.deck: Amit Varma, via Timur Kuran, on endowments that outlived their purpose
body: A waqf, Amit Varma said, was a marvellous innovation: a rich man’s endowment for a fixed public purpose, forever. He called it “the voluntary private provision of public goods”, with no coercion and no taxation. {021-C20}

But the purpose could never change. Timur Kuran’s example is a caravanserai, a roadside inn, founded on the Silk Route in the mid-1200s. By the 1600s nobody used the route, yet the money could not be moved: it was what Hernando de Soto would call dead capital, Varma said. {021-S07}
Another waqf built water fountains, thirty a year. {#thirty} Once piped water spread, the need was for better pipes, but the funds were tied to fountains.

quote.text: But you’re not allowed to shift the funds out of the caravanserai, right? So they are kind of stuck there.

second.caption: the waqf that funded a caravanserai

third.head: Small town, first class
body: Ravi Narayan, one of the founding team of NSE, had a line that Ajay Shah called beautiful: when satellite communications for NSE trading first reached a small town in India, it was like a railway line arriving there for the first time. {021-S05}
Before that, an investor in such a town had to place long-distance trunk calls to a Bombay broker. Then, Shah said, “Suddenly everybody was an equal first class participant.”

NSE, he said, was a global pioneer in electronic trading over satellite. Telecommunications was the first of the three pillars of modern finance, he said, since finance is “the business of bits and bytes”. {021-C13}
Today people trade on a mobile phone, he noted, which would have seemed miraculous only a short while ago.
third.caption: the satellite that came like a railway

p2.title: The layers of finance
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s history of finance, one felt need at a time, and Amit Varma on the Middle East’s stagnation

sections.label: The first layer
sections.head: When my ship comes in
sections.caption: the ship that might not come in
body: A thousand years ago, Ajay Shah said, finance was simple: money lent to people you knew, with unlimited liability. If you failed, the lenders came after your house, and if that was not enough, you went to debtors’ prison.

Fitting out a ship for India was a vast expense in a Europe that was not yet rich, and about one ship in four was lost to cyclones, pirates or something else. Hence the English phrase “when my ship comes in”. {021-S02}
## Two inventions, one idea
The first answer was the joint stock company. Instead of five people pooling money, thousands could, each placing a bet they could afford to lose. {021-C04}

The second was limited liability. If the company failed, lenders got “the carcass of the company” and could not chase the shareholders. Without that cap, Shah said, you cannot attract thousands of investors; the two ideas go together.
Amit Varma argued that it helps lenders too: more ships mean better shipbuilding, economies of scale and more bright minds.

In India, Shah said, these ideas have not yet sunk in. Regulators get unhappy when a share goes to zero, and populists want promoters to pay a failed company’s debts. “If you’re not missing any flights, you’re going too early,” he said. {021-C05}
~ Separating money from ideas quickened capitalism, he added. The economist John Hicks said the Industrial Revolution was as much about the stock market as the steam engine. {021-J11}

quote.text: Because if your ship came in, you were very rich. But there was a very high chance that your ship would not come in.

sections.label: The second layer
sections.head: Bulls, bears and free speech
sections.caption: the price as a public good
body: Once there were many shareholders, Ajay Shah said, the next step was natural: “Can I not sell them to you?” So trading began, bringing two pieces of magic.

The first was liquidity. No two flats are alike, and selling gold means haggling over purity. Cut Infosys into a billion identical shares and an owner can sell tomorrow. “It was a revolution in world history,” Shah said. {021-C07}
The second was a public price. When software companies are valued highly, it beckons entrepreneurs to build another; when an industry trades poorly, the market shouts at them to stay away. {021-C08}
## The right to disagree

If you think a share is overpriced but do not own it, you can borrow it, sell it and buy it back later. Short selling, Shah said, is a kind of freedom of speech: you can say a security is too cheap, or too dear. {021-C09}

Every such trade is voluntary, and each side thinks it got the better deal. Short selling adds more of these double thank-you moments, since the long-term holder earns a rental fee for lending the share. {021-C10}
Amit Varma said that blaming short sellers when things go wrong is shooting the messenger.
~ He likened markets to chess, which the player Levon Aronian called a conversation. The market, Varma said, is “a symphony of voices expressing opinions”.

quote.text: It is a voluntary transaction between consenting adults, and there’s a double thank you moment there.

sections.label: The third layer
sections.head: Side bets on the main bets
sections.caption: the three pillars of modern finance
body: Banks, Ajay Shah said, are magical and fragile at once. With heavy leverage they create, out of thin air, an illusion of liquidity and of funding long-dated assets with short-dated deposits. He quoted the economist Merton Miller, who called banking “a disaster-prone 19th century industry”. {021-C12}
Because politicians will not let grandmothers and dentists lose their money, banking turns political. Shah is not optimistic that the problem can be solved.
## Three pillars

After 1947 the miracles began. Telecommunications connected markets, computation took over bookkeeping and calculation, and academic economics supplied knowledge about portfolios, risk and diversification. {021-C13}
The greatest flowering, Shah said, was derivatives, “a system of side bets on the main bets”, which let people with knowledge but little capital join in price discovery. {021-C15}

They are not new. Shah recalled a speech at the Bombay Stock Exchange about the late 19th century, which said the natives were “as good as anybody in the world on trading in put and call options”. {021-S06}
~ Algorithmic trading, he said, simply hands a human’s rule to a tireless clerk in code. “It won’t take a break to have chai, it won’t have a bad hair day.” {021-J09}

quote.text: We got technologies of communication, we got technologies of computation, and we got great explosions of human knowledge.

sections.label: The detour
sections.head: Too fair to get rich
sections.caption: the Middle East’s long divergence
body: Around 1000 AD, Amit Varma said, the Middle East’s economy was very similar to Europe’s. Then it stagnated until the middle of the 19th century, while Europe zoomed ahead. {021-C18}

Timur Kuran, who once taught Ajay Shah, demolishes three usual explanations. Islam was not hostile to commerce: Muslim traders dominated trading hubs. The region did innovate, in government institutions and taxation. And it was not incurious, as the historian Bernard Lewis argued: it kept up with military textbooks, but never took up economic ones.
## The irony of fairness

Islamic inheritance law was more equitable than primogeniture in Northern Europe, where the eldest son got everything. Two-thirds went to the extended family and the rest to sons and daughters, a daughter getting half a son’s share. {#twothirds}

But when a partner died, his share was spread among many heirs. So partnerships stayed small and brief, joint stock companies never formed, and nor did the laws and accounting that grow around them. Europe’s rule was, in Varma’s words, a “shitty law, completely unfair, but at least you know that there is a successor”. {021-C19}
~ Varma drew no prescriptive lesson, he said, only an appreciation of the complexity of the world.

quote.text: Now the central question of The Long Divergence is that circa a thousand AD, the Middle East economically was very similar to Europe.

side.boxText: Amit Varma paused mid-episode to recommend Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, a masterpiece, he said, and perhaps the most important essay of the last century: prices carry information that no central planner can ever gather. {021-R03}

contQuote.text: The role in shaping resource allocation in the real economy and in shaping prices in the financial economy should go to the people with the knowledge and not the people who have inherited family wealth.

stories.caption: why Europe risked death for pepper
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah answers a puzzle from his childhood
stories.head: A matter of life and pepper
body: As a child, Ajay Shah never understood why Europeans would board a ship with a 25 per cent chance of dying on every voyage, just to get pepper. “I could just have salt on my omelette,” he said.
The answer, he said, was the winter. Europe’s population had grown to the limit of what its farms could carry, and the only way to survive the cold months was to store meat from the summer. {021-S01}

And meat rots. “So you had exactly two choices,” Shah said. “You would either eat rotten meat, which is subjectively not a pleasant experience, and you would then suffer disease and die. Or you could have spices in order to preserve the meat.”

Then, in 1453, the Ottoman Empire conquered Istanbul and cut off the land route for spices from Asia, above all India. {#istanbul} Europe now had to find a sea route, and the great age of exploration began.

The Portuguese worked their way, as Shah put it, almost to the edge of South America, back down the Cape of Good Hope and up to Madagascar. There, “lo and behold”, they landed on a Malay who knew how to ride the monsoon currents to Calicut.
That was the start of the spice trade, and of a financial puzzle. A ship that came home made its backers very rich; one lost to a cyclone or pirates paid them nothing. {021-S02}
~ In a Europe that was not yet rich, no one person could stake that much on a single voyage. From that pressure, Shah said, came the first great financial innovations.
stories.why: Behaviour that looks irrational from outside often answers a life-or-death constraint. Rebuild the problem people faced, Shah’s method says, and history makes sense; so does finance, whose institutions began as answers to such real problems. {021-C01}
stories.postscript: Varma’s proposed title for a history of the world: *From Pepper to Peppa Pig*. Shah had never heard of Peppa Pig. {021-J03}

stories.start: So famously, uh Reuters became a very, very uh successful. Was it an organization?
stories.end: And that is how that information started going into prices.
stories.caption: Reuters and the pigeons of Waterloo
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why getting the news first is no crime
stories.head: News by pigeon post
body: Reuters, Ajay Shah said, made its name with pigeons. Unsure whether Reuters was then an organisation or a person, he told how it was the first to carry news of the Battle of Waterloo back to London, where it could be used for trading. {021-S04}
It was make or break: would Britain win or lose? Fortunes hung on the answer, and Reuters got it to a trading venue first.

In India, Shah said, people would whine that this was unfair access to information. He saw it differently: “That was the innovation, that was their contribution, that they actually created a novel pathway to that information.”
~ That, he said, is how information gets into prices: everyone’s knowledge is pooled in a public price, and anyone who disagrees can put their money where their mouth is.
stories.why: A faster channel for news is a contribution, not cheating: it is how information reaches the price. The same logic, Shah argued, defends short sellers, who let the bearish view into the price too. {021-C09}

stories.start: I have a funny story. Long ago in the early years of NSE
stories.end: And this is a decentralized, distributed, voluntary information system. There's no coercion.
stories.caption: the factory on fire
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on news that rushes into prices
stories.head: Smoke signals for the market
body: In the early years of NSE, Ajay Shah wandered the country teaching. Somewhere near Coimbatore, a man told him a story. {021-S03}

He was riding his two-wheeler past a factory when he saw smoke coming out of it: the factory was on fire. His response: “I hit the gas and I ran to the nearest NSE broker and I sold all my shares in that company.”

Shah called it a funny story, and it shows the price system at work. Whoever stumbles on news has a reason to push it into the price, and nobody has to order them to. “This is a decentralised, distributed, voluntary information system,” he said. “There’s no coercion.”
~ It is the same machinery that, Shah had said earlier, makes a share price a public good: a readout anyone can consult almost free. {021-C08}

quote.text: Now just see the incentives for information to turn into the price.

stories.start: Now I had done an episode last year with Mukulika Banerjee
stories.end: They were organic and they emerged from within.
stories.caption: Mukulika Banerjee’s ten-year question
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recommendation, and a decade in the Frontier
stories.head: The question that kept her up
body: In the late 1980s, Mukulika Banerjee was wondering whether to do a PhD. The advice she got was this: “Only do a PhD if there is a question that keeps you awake at night.” {021-S08}

Her question was about the Pathans, stereotyped as violent. How had the nonviolent Khudai Khidmatgar, led by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Frontier Gandhi, come out of them? The movement was wiped out after Partition.
She spent ten years on the book, travelling from village to village in the North-West Frontier Province in search of elders who had once been members. {#tenyears}
~ Her finding, Amit Varma said, was profound: the Pathans’ nonviolence was not imported from the West, nor from Gandhi. “They were organic and they emerged from within.”
stories.why: Good scholarship starts with a question you cannot let go of, and patient fieldwork can overturn a stereotype. Varma said her book, out around 2001, deserved far wider readership than it got. {021-R16}
stories.postscript: Served each home’s one prized chicken, she felt guilty, so, despite being a Hindu, she began eating beef instead. {021-S09}

quiz.q: Why, by Ajay Shah’s account, did Europeans risk death at sea for pepper?
quiz.a: To preserve meat stored through winter; the alternative was eating rotten meat and falling ill.

quiz.q: How did Reuters first make its name, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: By using pigeons to carry news of the Battle of Waterloo to London first.

quiz.q: A man near Coimbatore saw a factory on fire. What did he do?
quiz.a: He sped to the nearest NSE broker and sold all his shares in that company.

quiz.q: Which economist did Shah quote as calling banking a disaster-prone 19th century industry?
quiz.a: Merton Miller, quoted to show that banks are magical but fragile at the core.

quiz.q: What did a waqf built for a Silk Route caravanserai end up as?
quiz.a: Dead capital: by the 1600s nobody used the route, but the funds could not move.
